summary: Defines a mechanism by which TCP/UDP-based clients can access the OSI Directory Service without the overhead of the ISO transport and presentation protocols needed for full DAP. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary:
DIXIE is a small protocol that stands in front of the X.500 directory. A tiny client sends a short request to a DIXIE server, which does the real directory work using the full protocol and sends back the answer.

Because it is just a translation, DIXIE covers the same operations as the directory itself: reading, searching, listing, and changing entries.

questions: what are the dixie operation codes
subtitle: A lightweight UDP and TCP gateway that lets small hosts query and edit the OSI X.500 Directory.

tldr.problem: The X.500 directory is reached through the Directory Access Protocol, which needs the full OSI stack and a lot of code. Small hosts, such as a Macintosh or a PC, could not afford to implement it.
tldr.mechanism: DIXIE translates the DAP operations into a simple sixteen-octet-header protocol carried over UDP or TCP. The server does the directory work, and the client speaks the simple protocol.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational document that provides information for the Internet community and says it does not specify any standard. Changes to the directory must be made over TCP.

sections.title: Why DIXIE Exists
sections.content:
The OSI Directory Service defines a powerful mechanism for storing and retrieving information about objects, and for arranging those objects in a hierarchical structure. Many types of objects and information can be stored in the directory, including white pages information, application information and service information. The OSI protocol defined to allow access to this information is the Directory Access Protocol. The DAP, being an OSI application-layer program, is fairly heavy-weight and requires a substantial amount of computing power and coding investment to implement.

The DIXIE protocol is designed for use by smaller hosts, such as Macintoshes and PCs, that do not have the computing power or the necessary software to implement a full OSI protocol stack. It is also useful for any Internet application that wants a simple interface to X.500 that requires very little coding investment.

The basic idea behind DIXIE is the same as that described in RFC 1202 for the Directory Assistance Protocol. DIXIE offers both UDP and TCP access to the directory. While the Directory Assistance Protocol exports something of a user interface, DIXIE provides a more direct protocol translation.

DIXIE follows a client-server request and response paradigm. Clients send request packets to a DIXIE server, and the server sends reply packets in return. Communication may be over UDP or TCP, depending on the needs of the client. All modification operations, that is ADD, REMOVE, MODIFY and MODIFYRDN, must be performed over a TCP connection, which provides some level of authentication.

Whichever method of communication is used, the general packet format is the same. Each packet consists of a sixteen octet header followed by some data. The representation used for all X.500 data passed between the server and the client is the QUIPU EDB format, so a Distinguished Name might look something like c=US@o=University of Michigan. The DIXIE server listens on port 96 for both UDP packets and TCP connections. The RFC notes that the protocol has evolved over time and that, without an understanding of the circumstances surrounding that evolution, the wisdom of some of the design decisions may not be apparent.
sections.plainLanguage: The idea is the same as for the Directory Assistance service, but sharper: instead of exporting a user interface, DIXIE exports the directory operations themselves, with a small fixed-size header in front of each one.

sections.title: The Sixteen-Octet Header
sections.content:
The DIXIE packet header is sixteen octets long. For requests it is laid out as follows. At offset 0, one octet holds an opcode specifying one of the operations. At offset 1, two octets hold a request identifier to be included in the reply, which should be unique to a request. At offset 3, four octets hold the total length of the request packet, excluding the header. Offset 7 has two unused octets. At offset 9, one octet holds options, of which there are currently only three: if bit 0 is set, large attributes will be included in the response, and the choice of what constitutes large is up to the implementation; if bit 1 is set, the dereference aliases service control will be set for the X.500 operation; and if bit 2 is set, aliases will not be dereferenced and searched during a search operation. At offset 10, one octet holds the protocol version, currently 1. At offset 11, one octet specifies the scope of a search. At offset 12, two octets hold a time limit in seconds for the operation, and at offset 14, two octets hold a size limit for the operation, used by search and list.

The reply header has the same length but a different arrangement. Offset 0 holds a return code specifying either success or describing any error that occurred. Offset 1 holds the two octets of the identifier included in the corresponding request packet. Offset 3 holds the four octets of the total length of the response packet, excluding the header. Offset 7 has three unused octets, offset 10 holds the protocol version, and offset 11 has five unused octets. All unused fields should be set to null octets and are reserved for future expansion.
sections.plainLanguage: Every request and reply starts with the same sixteen bytes: what to do, which request this is, how long the answer will be, and a few switches. The bytes in between are the directory data itself.

sections.title: The Eight Operations
sections.content:
The DIXIE operations closely parallel the X.500 DAP operations, and there are eight of them.

Read, opcode 0x01, asks for one entry. The data is the distinguished name of the entry to read, a null octet, and then a null-octet separated list of attributes whose values are to be returned. If no attributes are listed, all are returned, and the packet is terminated by two null octets in a row. The reply data is the entry read followed by a null octet: an entry consists of the distinguished name, the octet 0x02, and a list of attribute values separated by 0x02 octets, where an attribute value consists of an attribute type, the octet 0x01, and a list of values separated by 0x01 octets.

Search, opcode 0x0f, looks for entries under a given one. Octet 11 of the header gives the scope: 0x01 for a base object, 0x02 for one level, or 0x03 for the whole subtree. The data is the distinguished name of the entry to start from, a null octet, a string containing the search filter in dish-style, a null octet, and then a null-octet separated list of attributes to return. The reply begins with two octets in network byte order giving the number of matches, followed by that many sequences of one 0x03 octet and one entry.

List, opcode 0x10, names the subordinates of an entry. The request data is the distinguished name of the entry followed by a null octet, and the reply gives the number of subordinates returned and then that many sequences of a 0x03 octet and a relative distinguished name.

Modify, opcode 0x02, changes an entry. The data is the distinguished name of the entry, a null octet, and a null-separated list of modify operations: type removes an attribute type; type=value makes the value the sole value for the attribute type, deleting any existing values first; type+=value adds a value to the attribute type, creating the type if it does not already exist; and type-=value removes a value from the attribute type. The QUIPU EDB format used to specify the value allows multiple values separated by the ampersand character. This operation is only allowed over TCP, and there is no reply data, so the return code in the header is the only indication of success or failure.

Modify RDN, opcode 0x13, renames an entry. The data is the distinguished name of the entry to modify, a null octet, the new relative distinguished name, and a final null octet. The old value is never kept as an attribute of the entry. This operation is only allowed over TCP and again has no reply data.

Add, opcode 0x11, creates an entry. The data is the distinguished name of the new entry, a null octet, and a null-separated list of its attributes, each of the form type=value where the value can be a single value or several separated by the ampersand character. The request is terminated by two null octets. This operation is only allowed over TCP, with no reply data.

Remove, opcode 0x12, deletes an entry. The data is the distinguished name of the entry to remove followed by a null octet. This operation is only allowed over TCP, with no reply data.

Bind, opcode 0x04, corresponds to a DAP BIND using simple authentication as defined in Recommendation X.509. The data is the distinguished name of the entry as which to bind, a null octet, the password of that entry, and a final null octet. A null distinguished name causes a bind as NULLDN. The reply depends on the transport: over TCP there is no reply data and the return code alone says whether it worked, while over UDP the reply data is an Internet address in dot notation, the octet 0x01, a decimal number in text form, and a null octet, giving the address and port the client should connect to for an authenticated TCP connection bound as the entity named in the request.
sections.plainLanguage: Eight verbs, matching the directory's own: read one entry, search, list what is underneath, change an entry, rename it, add one, delete one, and log in. Anything that changes the directory has to go over TCP.

sections.title: Return Codes
sections.content: The return code in the reply header says whether the request succeeded or describes the error. There are seventeen values. 0x01 means the request was successful, and 0x02 that the search did not find any matches. 0x03 is some unknown, generic DIXIE error, and 0x04 that the opcode was not recognized by the DIXIE server. 0x05 means insufficient access to perform a modification, and 0x06 that a malformed distinguished name was supplied. 0x07 means some time limit or size limit was reached, in which case partial results will be returned. 0x08 means a modify was attempted before a bind. 0x09 means a fragment requested was not found, and 0x0a that an attribute type specified is invalid. 0x0b means an attribute specified does not exist in the entry, and 0x0c that an attribute value specification is invalid. 0x0d means an attribute value does not exist, as for removal of the value. 0x0e means a modification of an entry's relative distinguished name was attempted via a modify operation, which is not allowed, and modrdn should be used instead. 0x0f means a supplied distinguished name references an invalid portion of the tree. 0x10 means the Directory System Agent has passed back a referral to another DSA, as for a modification to a non-local entry, and the DIXIE server was unable to follow it. 0x11 means the DSA is down or unreachable.
sections.plainLanguage: Most of the codes say something practical: you have not logged in yet, that attribute is not there, the address you gave is not in the tree, or the directory server on the far side is down.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo says in one line that security issues are not discussed in it. It notes only that the modification operations have to be performed over a TCP connection, which provides some level of authentication, and that the bind operation carries a password in the simple form defined by Recommendation X.509.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo does not analyse security. It does insist that changes travel over TCP, and that a client identifies itself with a name and a password.

viz.caption: The DIXIE request header, as laid out in Section 2.1 of RFC 1249

fields.name: Request ID
fields.desc: Identifier included in the reply; should be unique to a request.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Total length of the request packet, excluding the header.

fields.name: Unused
fields.desc: Reserved for future expansion; set to null octets.

fields.name: Options
fields.desc: Bit 0 asks for large attributes, bit 1 sets dereference aliases, bit 2 suppresses dereferencing aliases in a search.

fields.name: Protocol Version
fields.desc: The protocol version in use. The current version is 1.

fields.name: Search Scope
fields.desc: For a search: base object, one level, or whole subtree.

fields.name: Timelimit
fields.desc: Time limit in seconds for the operation.

fields.name: Sizelimit
fields.desc: Size limit for the operation, used by search and list.

items.label: Read
items.desc: Return one entry and its attributes.

items.label: Modify
items.desc: Change the attributes of an entry. Only over TCP.

items.label: Bind
items.desc: Authenticate as an entry, with a name and a password.

items.label: Search
items.desc: Find entries under a given entry, with a filter and a scope.

items.label: List
items.desc: Name the subordinates of an entry.

items.label: Add
items.desc: Create a new entry. Only over TCP.

items.label: Remove
items.desc: Delete an entry. Only over TCP.

items.label: Modify RDN
items.desc: Rename an entry. Only over TCP.

items.label: Success
items.desc: The request was successful.

items.label: No matches
items.desc: The search did not find any matches.

items.label: Generic error
items.desc: Some unknown, generic DIXIE error has occurred.

items.label: Unknown opcode
items.desc: The opcode was not recognized by the DIXIE server.

items.label: Insufficient access
items.desc: Insufficient access to perform a modification.

items.label: Malformed DN
items.desc: A malformed distinguished name was supplied.

items.label: Limit reached
items.desc: A time limit or size limit was reached; partial results are returned.

items.label: Modify before bind
items.desc: A modify was attempted before a bind.

items.label: Fragment not found
items.desc: A fragment requested was not found.

items.label: Invalid attribute type
items.desc: An attribute type specified is invalid.

items.label: No such attribute
items.desc: An attribute specified does not exist in the entry.

items.label: Invalid value
items.desc: An attribute value specification is invalid.

items.label: No such value
items.desc: An attribute value does not exist, as for removal of the value.

items.label: Wrong operation
items.desc: A modification of an entry's relative distinguished name was attempted via a modify operation.

items.label: Invalid tree portion
items.desc: A supplied distinguished name references an invalid portion of the tree.

items.label: Referral not followed
items.desc: The DSA passed back a referral to another DSA and the DIXIE server could not follow it.

items.label: DSA unreachable
items.desc: The DSA is down or unreachable.
